en: [ACT IV]
(Same set as in the First Act.)
[SCENE I]

OSMONDE, EDMÉE, then FÉLICIE : (Osmonde is seated, reading; from time to time she casts a glance at her mother who is also seated, dressed for going out, looking distraught, and has not even taken off her hat.)
OSMONDE : Are you going out again?
EDMÉE : No.
OSMONDE : Then why don't you take off your hat? (Edmée slowly removes her hat. A silence.) Do you intend to keep it on your lap for long? (A knock at the door.) Come in. What is it, Félicie?
FÉLICIE, entering : Madame hasn't ordered anything for dinner.
EDMÉE : Do whatever you like.
FÉLICIE : Oh! But I wouldn't know; it's for Madame to say.
EDMÉE : Well, the same as yesterday.
FÉLICIE : And the boarder who already came to tell me this morning that he can't stomach spinach!
OSMONDE : You shouldn't say "the boarder," Félicie... You are not to take complaints from that gentleman; if he isn't satisfied, it is to Madame that he must complain. Do you understand?
FÉLICIE : That's what I told him. He says Madame intimidates him—how should I know?
OSMONDE : Run along, Félicie.
FÉLICIE : So, that's settled then? I'll make the same thing as yesterday. Don't go complaining that it's always the same. (She goes out.)
[SCENE II]
EDMÉE, OSMONDE : (A silence.)
OSMONDE, without looking up : Is he dead?
EDMÉE : What are you saying?
OSMONDE : I'm asking if he's dead.
EDMÉE : Whom are you talking about?
OSMONDE : Why, about him... that gentleman from the other day.
EDMÉE : Osmonde!
OSMONDE : Well, I don't know, you see; I'm not used to seeing you so... depressed.
EDMÉE : Then your father told you...
OSMONDE : It would seem so.
EDMÉE : Why didn't he tell me he had spoken to you? When did this happen?
OSMONDE : Two days ago.
EDMÉE : And you, you didn't even...
OSMONDE : I really don't know what one says in such a case; I suppose there are formulas, but those, you never taught me.
EDMÉE : You have no heart.
OSMONDE : That is nothing new.
EDMÉE : Generous as he is, I am quite sure that your father...
OSMONDE : He confined himself to informing me of a fact that requires no comment.
EDMÉE : Close your book, please.
OSMONDE : If it gives you pleasure. (She closes her book, turns toward her mother, and looks at her, elbow resting on the table.)
EDMÉE : I don't have to enter into details.
OSMONDE : I might point out, for that matter, that I haven't asked you for anything.

EDMÉE : But what you can tell yourself is that three human beings have suffered mortally through one another, without it being perhaps the fault of any one of them, and that it isn't over. Do you hear what I am saying?
OSMONDE : Naturally, but I don't see what any of that has to do with me.
EDMÉE : Someone young like you, someone with life before her...
OSMONDE : Oh!
EDMÉE : Ought to feel the desire to bring a little comfort to... these unfortunate souls.
OSMONDE : I don't grasp your meaning.
EDMÉE : That person you were speaking of...
OSMONDE : The gentleman from the other day?
EDMÉE : He has only a very short time left to live.
OSMONDE, coldly : That is very sad.
EDMÉE : But surely you know who he is? He is your...
OSMONDE : And so?
EDMÉE : He has no one with him but a hired nurse... (Her shoulders are shaken by a kind of convulsive sob.)
OSMONDE : Listen, Mother, I remind you that young Junod may come in at any moment; if he sees that face...
EDMÉE : What do you expect me to care?
OSMONDE : Ah! I thought that under all circumstances one had to "keep up appearances."

EDMÉE : At your age one cannot even conceive what a certain loneliness can be; when one is no longer young, when one is sick and there is perhaps not a single happy memory in all the past to look back on...
OSMONDE : Oh? That gentleman has no pleasant memories?
EDMÉE : It would do him so much good if you would go and keep him company now and then. I can do nothing for him; he even says that I hurt him. (She can barely contain herself. A knock at the door.)
OSMONDE : Who is it?
[SCENE III]
THE SAME, FRED
FRED : I beg your pardon, Mademoiselle, above all I wouldn't want to disturb you. It really is of no importance... it was only to say... I don't know if you know that I had enteritis as a child.
OSMONDE : No, we did not know.
FRED : Yes, naturally; and so something of it stayed with me... Well, there are certain vegetables that I don't... so, passing by the kitchen, I thought I smelled...
OSMONDE : Very well, we'll make you an egg.
FRED : Thank you, Mademoiselle. I hope it won't be too much trouble; I do apologize, but my mother urged me so strongly... Besides, in our family, we all have delicate intestines.
OSMONDE : Yes, yes, goodbye. (Fred goes out.)
[SCENE IV]

OSMONDE : Now I confess I am very astonished at what you are asking of me. Even supposing I could find an hour here or there to go read aloud to that gentleman, I don't quite see what subjects of conversation we could have; I should hate to awaken painful memories, and since he has no other kind...
EDMÉE : That mocking tone is atrocious. You are a monster.
OSMONDE : You didn't let me finish my sentence. It would be elementary to ask Papa what he thinks of these visits.
EDMÉE : Your father is goodness itself.
OSMONDE : He is still deeply shaken.
EDMÉE : What do you mean?
OSMONDE : One does not make such a discovery with impunity.
EDMÉE : What discovery? What on earth are you imagining? He has known the truth for nineteen years.
OSMONDE : Oh? (A silence.)
[SCENE V]
THE SAME, FRED

FRED, half-opening the door : Mademoiselle, I only wanted to say that if by any chance someone is kind enough to make me an egg, it might be better if it weren't soft-boiled, because I thought I noticed that in Paris... But of course, whatever you wish. (Catching sight of Edmée.) Oh! Is Madame Lemoyne unwell? I am so sorry...
OSMONDE : My mother has a severe neuralgia. Mother, I think you should go lie down for a moment.
FRED : If I might venture... perhaps a powder would give your mother some relief, I have a little travel medicine chest that's quite well stocked...
EDMÉE : Thank you, Monsieur, you are very kind. (She goes out.)
[SCENE VI]

FRED : I'm afraid it was I who drove Madame Lemoyne away... I must have seemed so ridiculous to you with my spinach and my soft-boiled egg. I'm sure you're going to think that I only care about food. But it's quite the contrary; Mother will tell you that I never know what I'm eating. It's true, I have no fussy demands; besides, at home everyone considers me an intellectual.
OSMONDE : I see.

FRED : If I attached any importance to such things, I wouldn't have come to board at your parents' house. Because superior people like them eat just any old way... I was anxious to explain, because I would be quite distressed if you were left with that impression. A first impression is so important. To be sure, it isn't the first time circumstances have brought us together. Do you remember that summer you spent at Évilard at the Soldanelles boarding house? I was staying at the Hôtel des Cyclamens with my cousins from Le Locle... You had a smashing tennis stroke. We even played singles once, if you remember. And then there was that little party at the pension; you sang a little piece: it was splendid. As for me, music has such an effect on me! The tune has stayed with me ever since; if there were a piano, I'd play it for you.
OSMONDE : You have an excellent memory, which must be of great help to you in your studies.

FRED : Quite good enough. But there are things that aren't easy. Nowadays they ask of you so much erudition and philology and heaps of paraphernalia: there's no end to it. I don't know if you feel as I do, but I find that none of that ought to be necessary. What is needed, above all, is to have faith. As for me, I can't complain; I can truly say I have an enormous amount of faith—an enormous amount.
OSMONDE : My congratulations.
FRED : Oh, don't mention it. It's just my nature.
[SCENE VII]
THE SAME, CLAUDE
CLAUDE, to Fred : Good afternoon, Fred.
FRED, blushing : Good afternoon, Monsieur, I apologize for disturbing you; I had just come to ask Mademoiselle Osmonde a question.
CLAUDE : No harm done. (Fred goes out.)
OSMONDE : There you are: that is probably the sort of character I would have had the good fortune to stumble upon, if... Will you excuse me, Papa? (She sits down at the table and writes.)
CLAUDE : To whom are you writing?
OSMONDE : I'll tell you in a second... (She seals the letter and goes to the door.) Félicie!
FÉLICIE, offstage : Mademoiselle...
OSMONDE : Take this immediately to Monsieur Mégal's.
FÉLICIE, enters and takes the letter : Very well, Mademoiselle. (She goes out.)
CLAUDE : What does this mean?

OSMONDE : Now, tell me, Papa, I've just discovered... why did you let me believe you had only just learned the truth? I don't quite understand, and I confess I don't think it very fair of you. When I was hoping we would trust each other more from now on...
CLAUDE, in a low voice, without looking at her : It was out of cowardice that I lied to you.
OSMONDE : What?
CLAUDE : The thought that you would make certain reflections.
OSMONDE : What reflections? (A silence. Osmonde examines him.)
CLAUDE, very low : Reflections humiliating to me...
OSMONDE : Then I had understood.
CLAUDE : Where is your mother?
OSMONDE : She is lying on her bed.
CLAUDE : Is she ill? (An evasive gesture from Osmonde.) What is the matter with her?
OSMONDE : She seems rather demoralized to me.
CLAUDE : Did you speak of that?
OSMONDE : A few words.
CLAUDE, harshly : Yet I had forbidden you to.
OSMONDE : She was the one who approached me about that gentleman. She is asking me to go keep him company from time to time.
CLAUDE, violently : You will not go.
OSMONDE : I have no intention of going.
CLAUDE : I forbid you, it's as simple as that.
OSMONDE : You can spare yourself that trouble.
CLAUDE : And if by any chance he presumes to return...
OSMONDE : That is hardly likely.
CLAUDE : That would be the last straw, for you to go to his home without my permission!
OSMONDE : But, Papa, I don't know what has come over you.
CLAUDE : It's just that after all that has happened you might think, I don't know... but it's over, I guarantee you.
OSMONDE : What is over?
CLAUDE : I have humiliated myself enough. Ah! To hurt someone!
OSMONDE : You couldn't.
CLAUDE : Oh yes, now I would know how... Throw someone out... strike him.
OSMONDE : It would give you no pleasure.

CLAUDE, in an altered voice : That is what I have come to. Me. It is as if I had drunk alcohol... ah! It's frightening. For two days now. All the feelings I had never had, all the words I had never spoken... If you had heard earlier the sentences I was uttering almost out loud. Tell me that it will pass... But no, I am not even sure I want it to pass.
OSMONDE : You are beside yourself, that is obvious. But it is an outburst that will not last.
CLAUDE : Yes.
OSMONDE : Besides, there are moments when you are completely calm, it's only when you are alone...
CLAUDE : They are like surges rising up from I don't know where.
OSMONDE : You see, you are completely calm again.
CLAUDE : You speak to me as to a sick man.
FÉLICIE, outside : It's Monsieur Mégal, asking if he may speak to Mademoiselle.
CLAUDE : What?
OSMONDE : Show Monsieur Mégal in.
CLAUDE : Did you tell him to come?
OSMONDE : Yes.
[SCENE VIII]
THE SAME, MÉGAL
MÉGAL, bowing : Monsieur. Mademoiselle...

OSMONDE : I am glad that my father is present at our conversation. You told me you were looking for someone who could take complete charge of Yvonne and Suzanne. Well, I have come to offer to devote myself to them...
MÉGAL : Mademoiselle, I am more touched than I can say by your offer; but it is impossible... in the first place, you do not have the time.
CLAUDE : I cannot understand why you have troubled Monsieur Mégal for such an absurdity.
OSMONDE : All my time is free, and I need a task that will absorb me completely. The greatest service you could do me would be to accept the offer I am making you.
MÉGAL : But really, Mademoiselle, I do not know if you have considered that I am preparing to leave Paris for several months.
OSMONDE : You told me.
MÉGAL : Your parents...
